To variegate something means to make it varied in appearance by giving it patches, streaks, spots, or areas of different colors or markings. In other words, you take something and introduce visual diversity into it — breaking up uniformity with contrasting colors or patterns.

Think of it this way: if you have a plain green leaf and nature adds random splashes of white and yellow onto it, nature has variegated that leaf. The leaf is no longer one solid color. It now has variety built into its surface.
The Key Visual Quality It Implies

This is important: variegating is not the same as blending or mixing colors smoothly together (like a sunset gradient). When something is variegated, you can see distinct patches or streaks — the colors sit alongside each other, clearly visible as separate areas, not blurred or fused into one.

Imagine a cow with large black patches on a white body. That's a variegated appearance. Now compare that to a gray wall, where black and white paint have been mixed together into one uniform color. That is not variegated. The distinction matters.

So the word carries the idea of visible, recognizable variety — you can actually see the different colors or markings as separate things on the surface.
How It's Used in a Sentence

• "Autumn variegates the forest with reds, oranges, and yellows."
    → Autumn is the one doing the action. It takes the forest and marks different parts of it with different colors.
  • "The weaver variegated the cloth with bold stripes of blue, gold, and crimson."
    → The weaver deliberately introduced different colors into the fabric.
  • "Disease had variegated the rose petals with pale streaks."
    → The disease marked the petals with streaks of a different color.

In every case, notice the structure: something (or someone) acts on a surface and introduces visible color variety into it.

While color and visual appearance is the primary and most common use, "variegate" can occasionally be used in a wider sense to mean to make something generally diverse or varied — not just in color, but in character, content, or nature.

For example: "She variegated her lectures with anecdotes, experiments, and debates so that students wouldn't get bored."

Here, she is introducing variety into her lectures. No colors are involved — the word is being stretched to mean "make more varied and less monotonous." This usage is less common and more literary, but you may encounter it, so it's worth knowing.

In real life, you will come across the adjective form — "variegated" — far more often than the verb itself. When a plant has leaves with patches of white, cream, or yellow mixed with green, it is called a variegated plant. Garden centers and botanists use this word constantly.

"She bought a variegated ivy whose leaves were deep green edged with bright white."

Knowing the verb gives you a deeper understanding of the adjective: a variegated leaf is simply a leaf that has been variegated — marked with patches of different colors, whether by nature or otherwise.
A Way to Lock It in Your Memory

Connect the word to its closest everyday relative: variety. Both words share the same root idea. To variegate is essentially to build variety into something's appearance. If you can remember variegate = inject visual variety, you will never confuse or forget this word.
